Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verses 1–2:

(p-68) Surat Luqman

(Meccan, though it is said: except for "Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat," for their obligation was in Medina; but this is weak, since it contradicts their legislation in Mecca. It is also said: except for three verses from His saying: "And if all the trees on earth were pens..." and it has thirty-four verses.)

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ Its explanation has already passed in its counterparts.

﴿the Wise﴾ i.e., possessing wisdom, because it includes it. Or it is a description of it by His attribute, may He be exalted. Or its original form is "the Wise one who sent it down" or "the Wise one who spoke it," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifying noun was put in its place, and it became marfu' (nominative), hence it took a pronoun within the attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). It is also said: "al-Hakim" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'al, as they said: "I made the milk thick (a'qadtu al-laban), so it is 'aqid," i.e., mu'qad. This is rare. It is also said: it has the sense of fa'il.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verses 1–2:

(p-68) Surat Luqman

(Meccan, though it is said: except for "Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat," for their obligation was in Medina; but this is weak, since it contradicts their legislation in Mecca. It is also said: except for three verses from His saying: "And if all the trees on earth were pens..." and it has thirty-four verses.)

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ Its explanation has already passed in its counterparts.

﴿the Wise﴾ i.e., possessing wisdom, because it includes it. Or it is a description of it by His attribute, may He be exalted. Or its original form is "the Wise one who sent it down" or "the Wise one who spoke it," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifying noun was put in its place, and it became marfu' (nominative), hence it took a pronoun within the attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). It is also said: "al-Hakim" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'al, as they said: "I made the milk thick (a'qadtu al-laban), so it is 'aqid," i.e., mu'qad. This is rare. It is also said: it has the sense of fa'il.

﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ are in the accusative (naṣb) as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl, "circumstantial accusative") of "the verses" (al-āyāt), and the element governing both is the sense of indication (maʿnā al-ishārah). They are also read in the nominative (rafʿ), as two further predicates (khabarān) of the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), or of an elided subject (mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf, "elided subject").

﴿for the good-doers﴾: i.e., those who perform good deeds (al-ʿāmilīna lil-ḥasanāt). If by them are meant their well-known forms recognized in the religion, then His saying, exalted is He,

﴿Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat, and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ is an explanation (bayan, elaboration) of the good deeds they performed, following the manner of his saying:

؎ The man of keen insight who guesses about you the guess, ∗∗∗ as if he had seen and heard.

If by them is meant all good deeds, then it is a specification of these three by mentioning them among the rest of their branches, to show their excellence and their superiority over others. And specifying the first aspect to the case where the relative clause (mawsul) is a qualifying attribute (sifah) of "the doers of good," and the last aspect to the case where it is a subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence), is something without basis.

Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful (al-muflihun).

The successful are those who attain every sought-after goal and are saved from every feared thing, by virtue of their possessing both aspects of knowledge and action. What is said about this in the opening of Surah al-Baqarah has already passed, in a manner that cannot be improved upon.

(p-69) [Its position] (maḥalluhu) is in the nominative (rafʿ) as the subject (mubtada'), with respect to its content, or by supposing a noun it modifies (mawṣūf) to be omitted. The *man* (مَن) in His words, ﴿who purchases idle talk﴾, is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), or a qualifying noun (mawṣūfa) whose position is nominative as the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: "And some of mankind," or "and some of mankind, those who purchase," or "a group who purchase," on the basis that the point of the statement and its primary purpose is their being characterized by what is in the relative clause (ṣila) or the qualifying phrase (ṣifa), not their being those particular persons mentioned, as was explained in His words, ﴿And among mankind is he who says, "We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾ ... and the verses.

*Lahw al-ḥadīth* (idle talk) is that which diverts from what is important and worthwhile, such as baseless narratives, myths that carry no weight, amusing jests, and all other speech devoid of good, which are vain words. The genitive construction (iḍāfa) carries the sense of *min* (explanatory, "of") if by *ḥadīth* is meant the reprehensible, and the sense of *min* (partitive, "some of") if by it is meant the more general, including that. It has been said: the verse was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who bought the books of the non-Arabs (a'ājim) and would relate them to the Quraysh, saying: "If Muḥammad (ﷺ) relates to you the story of ʿĀd and Thamūd, then I will relate to you the story of Rustam, Isfandiyār, and the Kisrās (Persian kings)." It has also been said: he used to buy singing girls (qiyān) and bring them to keep company with anyone who wished to embrace Islam, to keep him away from it.

﴿to lead astray from the way of God﴾, i.e., His true religion, which conveys one to Him; or from the recitation (qirāʾa, a mode of reading) of His Book, which guides to Him. It is read as (*liyaḍilla*) with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ*, meaning: that he may remain and persist in his error, or that he may increase in it.

﴿without knowledge﴾, i.e., regarding the state of what he purchases, or regarding the trade, in that he exchanged pure evil for pure good.

﴿and take it﴾ in the accusative (naṣb), conjoined to *yuḍilla*, and the pronoun refers to *al-sabīl* (the way), for it is of the type that may be masculine or feminine, and it is the religion of Islam, or the Qur'an; i.e., and that he may take it.

﴿as a mockery﴾, i.e., made an object of mockery. It is also read as (*wa-yattakhidhu*) with a *ḍamma* (nominative), conjoined to "yashtarī" (purchases). His words, ﴿those﴾, refer to *man*; the plural is in regard to its meaning, just as the singular in the two verbs is in regard to its wording. The sense of distance contained in it, despite the recent mention of the one referred to, serves to announce the remoteness of their rank in wickedness; i.e., those characterized by what was mentioned of purchasing for the purpose of misguidance.

﴿For them is a humiliating punishment﴾, because of their being characterized by humiliating the truth by preferring falsehood over it and by enticing people toward it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 7:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to him﴾ i.e., to the purchaser. The pronoun in it, and in what follows it, is singular, like the first three pronouns, with regard to the wording of the phrase (lafz), after it had been plural between them with regard to its meaning (ma'na).

﴿Our verses﴾, which are the verses of the Wise Book, and guidance, and a mercy for the good-doers.

﴿He turns away﴾ i.e., he turns away from them, not counting them of any worth.

﴿Arrogantly﴾ i.e., exaggerating in arrogance.

﴿As if he had not heard them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the pronoun of "turns away" or from the pronoun of "arrogantly". The original form is "ka-annahu" (as if he). The pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) was deleted and the heavy form was lightened, meaning: his state resembles the state of one who did not hear them, while he is in fact a hearer. In it is an allusion that one who has heard them cannot be imagined to turn away or be arrogant, because of what they contain of matters that necessitate turning towards them and submitting to them, in the manner of the saying of the one who said:

﴿As if you had not grieved over Ibn Tarif﴾

﴿As if there were heaviness in his ears﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "had not heard them", meaning: his state resembles the state of one who has in his ears a deafness preventing hearing. It is permissible that both be resumptive clauses (isti'nafayn). It was read: (fi udhnayhi) with the dhal sukun-ed.

﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾ i.e., inform him that a punishment extremely painful in its affliction will inevitably befall him. The mention of "tidings" is for mockery (tahakkum).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is an explanation of the state of the believers in His signs, exalted is He, following the explanation of the state of the disbelievers in them. That is: those who believe in His signs, exalted is He, and act in accordance with what they entail.

﴿For them﴾ in return for what was mentioned of their faith and their deeds.

﴿Gardens of bliss﴾ i.e., (p-70) the bliss of gardens. It is the inverted form (fa'kas, a rhetorical reversal) for emphasis. The clause is the predicate of inna (the khabar of inna). Yet the better view is that "lahum" (for them) be taken as the predicate, since "jannatu al-na'im" (gardens of bliss) is raised by it as the agent (fa'iliyyah, the subject of the verb-like predicate). And the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 9:

﴿Abiding therein forever.﴾ This is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, a state of the subject) either referring to the pronoun in "for them" (lahum), or referring to "gardens of bliss" (jannāt al-naʿīm), because it contains both of their pronouns; and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) is what the preposition (lām) is attached to.

﴿A promise of Allah, true.﴾ These are two infinitive absolutes (maṣdarān) serving as emphasis (muʾakkidān): the first emphasizes itself, and the second emphasizes something other than itself. This is because His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For them are gardens of bliss﴾ carries the meaning of "Allah has promised them gardens of bliss," so the meaning of promise is emphasized by a promise. As for "true" (ḥaqqan), it indicates the meaning of firmness and certainty, and by it the meaning of promise is emphasized. The thing emphasizing both of them together is ﴿for them are gardens of bliss﴾.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the One whom nothing overcomes, so as to prevent Him from fulfilling His promise or carrying out His threat.

﴿the Wise﴾: the One who does nothing except what wisdom (ḥikmah) and benefit (maṣlaḥah) require.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 10:

﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾ ... etc. It is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought to serve as evidence for what has been detailed concerning His exalted might (izza), which is the perfection of power, and His wisdom (hikma), which is the perfection of knowledge, and as a preparation for and affirmation of the principle of tawhid (divine oneness), and the nullification of the matter of association (shirk), and the rebuke of its adherents. "Amad" (pillars) is the plural of "imad" (support), like "ahab" is the plural of "ihab" (hide), and it is that by which something is propped up, i.e., supported. It is said: "I propped up the wall" (amadtu al-ha'it) when you buttressed it, i.e., without supports. The plural form is due to the multiplicity of the heavens. His exalted words: ﴿You see them﴾ are a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought in as evidence for what was mentioned of His creating them in a manner not customary, as witnessed by them seeing them in such a state; or it is a qualifier of "amad", i.e., He created them without pillars, visible; the restriction serves as an allusion that the pillar He supported them with, which you do not see, is the pillar of power. ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ is an explanation of His wondrous handiwork in the settling of the earth, following the explanation of His wise handiwork in the settling of the heavens, i.e., He cast into it stable mountains. What is involved in this has already been discussed in Surat al-Ra'd.

﴿Lest it should sway with you﴾ meaning lest it incline with you, for the simplicity of its parts requires the alteration of their places and positions, since it is impossible for each of them, by its essence or by some of its necessary attributes, to be specific to a particular place and a particular disposition.

﴿And He spread therein from every kind of creature (dabba)﴾ from every species of its kinds.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water﴾ which is rain.

﴿Then We caused to grow therein﴾ by means of that water.

﴿Of every noble pair﴾ of every kind of great benefit. The shift to the first-person plural ("We") in the two verbs is to show greater concern for the matter.

﴿This﴾, i.e., what was mentioned of the heavens and the earth and the countable matters connected with them.

﴿is the creation of Allah﴾, i.e., His creation.

﴿So show me what those besides Him have created﴾ of what you have taken as partners to Him, glorified is He, in worship, to the point that they deserved worship because of it. The word ﴿ماذا﴾ is either in the accusative, governed by ﴿خَلَقَ﴾, or it is in the nominative as the inceptive subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being ﴿ذا﴾ together with its relative clause (silah). The phrase ﴿أرُونِي﴾ is connected to it. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾, it is a turning away (idrab) from rebuking them with what has been mentioned, to recording upon them clear error. This calls for turning away from addressing them with rational, true premises, because it is impossible for them to understand anything from them so that they would be guided by it to knowledge of the falsity of what they hold, or be affected by the argument and rebuke so that they would desist from it. Placing the apparent noun in the position of their pronoun serves to indicate that by their association (of partners with God) they are (p-71) placing things in other than their proper place, transgressing the limits, and wronging themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 12:

﴿And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom﴾. This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to explain the invalidity of shirk (associating partners with God). He is Luqman son of Ba'ura' (Ba'uraʾ), of the descendants of Azar, the son of the sister of Job (Ayyub), peace be upon him, or his maternal aunt's son. He lived until he reached David, peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him, and he used to give legal rulings (yufti) before his prophetic mission (mab'ath). It is also said that he was a judge among the Children of Israel. The majority hold that he was a sage (hakim) and was not a prophet. Wisdom (hikmah), in the terminology of the scholars, is the perfecting of the human soul through acquiring theoretical sciences and gaining complete mastery over virtuous actions according to one's capacity. Among his wisdom: he accompanied David, peace be upon him, for months, and he would weave the coat of mail, and [David] did not ask him about it. When [David] finished it, he put it on and said: "How excellent a armour of war you are!" [Luqman] said: "Silence is wisdom, and few are those who practise it." David, peace be upon him, said to him: "Truly, you were rightly named a sage." And David, peace be upon him, once said to him: "How have you risen this morning?" He said: "I have risen in the hands of another." David reflected on this and swooned in a swoon. It is also reported that his Lord commanded him to slaughter a sheep and bring the two best morsels from it, so he brought the tongue and the heart. Then, after some days, He commanded him to bring the two most wicked morsels from it, so he brought those too. [David] asked him about that, and he said: "They are the best of things when they are good, and the worst of things when they are wicked."

﴿That give thanks to God﴾: the meaning is, give thanks to Him, the most high, where "that" (an) is explanatory (mufassirah), since the giving of wisdom carries the sense of saying. His, the most high, saying: ﴿And whoever gives thanks﴾ ... etc. is a resumed statement that confirms the content of what precedes it and makes obedience to the command obligatory; that is: and whoever gives thanks to Him, the most high.

﴿Then he gives thanks only for his own soul﴾, because his benefit, which is the binding of what is present and the drawing of what is increased, is confined to it.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is Self-Sufficient﴾ above everything, so He has no need of thanks, that He might be harmed by the disbelief of whoever disbelieves.

﴿Praiseworthy﴾: deserving of praise even if no one praises Him, or praised in act, all of creation speaking His praise with the tongue of state. The lack of mention of His being thanked, the most high, is because praise includes thanks, indeed it is its head, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Praise is the head of thanks; a servant who does not praise God has not thanked Him." So affirming it for Him, the most high, is definitively affirming thanks for Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 13:

﴿And when Luqman said to his son﴾ — An'am. It is also said: Ashkam. It is also said: Mathan.

﴿while he was admonishing him, "O my little son"﴾ — a diminutive expressing affection (tasghir al-ishfaq). It is also read (Ya bunayya) with the yaʾ pronounced quiescent (bi-iskan al-yaʾ) and with it vocalised with a kasra (bi-kasriha).

﴿Do not associate anything with Allah﴾ — It is said: his son was a disbeliever, and he kept at him until he embraced Islam. Whoever pauses at "do not associate" makes "by Allah" an oath.

﴿Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong﴾ — an explanation of the prohibition, or of the cessation from associating partners.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 14:

﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents⦆ ... etc. This is a resumed statement, inserted parenthetically in the course of Luqman's admonition by way of digression, as an emphasis on what it contains of the prohibition of associating partners with God. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His mother bore him﴾ up to His saying "in two years" is a parenthetical clause between the commentator and what is commented upon. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿weakness upon weakness﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to his mother, meaning: she bearing him in weakness. Or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing a verb that is the circumstantial clause, meaning: she grows weak with weakness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿upon weakness⦆ is a qualifier of the verbal noun, meaning: being upon weakness, that is, she weakens with a weakness upon weakness, for her weakness continues to double. It has also been read: "wahanan ʿalā wahanin" with vowelization (taḥrīk), it is said: wahana yahinu wahnan, and wahina yuhinu wahanan.

﴿And his weaning is in two years⦆, that is, his weaning is at the completion of two years, and this is the period of nursing according to al-Shafi'i. According to Abu Hanifa, may God Most High have mercy on them both, it is thirty months. He has explained its basis in its proper place. It has also been read: (wa-faṣluhu). ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents⦆ is an explanation of "We enjoined." What lies between them is a parenthetical clause emphasizing the injunction regarding her in particular, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the one who asked him, "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?": "Your mother, then your mother, then your mother," then he said after that: "Then your father." ﴿To Me is the final return⦆ is a reason for the obligation of compliance, meaning: the return is to Me and not to another, so I will recompense you for what proceeds from you of gratitude and ingratitude.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 15:

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them.﴾ That is: by their associating (partners) with Him, the Exalted, in the entitlement to worship.

﴿But do not obey them in that.﴾

﴿And accompany them in this world with kindness.﴾ That is: companionship that is good, which the Sharia approves and which good manners (muruwwa) require.

﴿And follow the way of him who turns back to Me (in repentance).﴾ By monotheism and sincerity in obedience.

﴿Then to Me is your return.﴾ That is: your return, and their return, and the return of him who turns back to Me.

﴿Then I will inform you﴾ when you return.

﴿of what you used to do.﴾ By recompensing each one of you for what proceeded from him of good and evil.

And His, the Exalted's, saying:

"O my son!" ... etc. This begins the narration of the rest of Luqman's admonitions, following the affirmation of what came at its opening, namely the prohibition of associating partners with God, and its emphasis by means of the parenthetical interjection.

﴿Indeed, it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾ That is: indeed, the deed, whether of evil or of good, if it be, by way of example, in smallness like a mustard seed. It has also been read with the noun "weight" (mithqal) in the nominative, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the matter (al-qissah), and the verb "kana" is complete (taamma), and the feminine form is due to the attachment of "weight" to "grain" (habbah), as in the saying of one who said: "As the spear's head became stained with blood." Or because what is meant by it is the good deed or the bad deed.

﴿Then it will be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth﴾ That is: then it will be, despite being in the utmost degree of smallness and insignificance, in the most hidden and most secure place, such as the hollow of a rock, or wherever it may be, in the upper world or the lower world.

﴿God will bring it forth﴾ That is: He will produce it and call to account for it.

﴿Indeed God is Subtle﴾ whose knowledge reaches every hidden thing, ﴿Aware﴾ of its essence. Having commanded him to monotheism, which is the first thing obligatory upon a person, within the context of the prohibition of associating partners, and having alerted him to the perfection of God's knowledge and power, he commanded him to prayer, which is the most perfect of the acts of worship, thereby completing him in respect of action after completing him in respect of belief, and so he said, seeking to incline him towards it:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 17:

﴿O my dear son, establish the prayer﴾ as a perfecting of yourself.

﴿And enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ as a perfecting of others.

﴿And bear patiently what befalls you﴾ of hardships and trials, especially in what you have been commanded to do.

﴿Indeed, that﴾ is a reference to (p-73) all that has been mentioned. The sense of distance in it, despite the recency of the thing referred to, is because of what has passed many times of indicating the loftiness of its rank in excellence.

﴿Of the matters requiring resolve﴾ i.e., of the matters that Allah the Exalted has resolved upon and decreed for His servants, owing to their great excellence. It is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul). It has also been permitted that it means the active participle (fa'il), from the words of the Exalted: ﴿فَإذا عَزَمَ الأمْرُ﴾ ("when the matter is resolved upon"), i.e., became serious. The sentence is a justification for the obligation to comply with the commands and prohibitions mentioned before it, and an indication that what follows it is not on the same level.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 18:

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾ That is: do not incline it, and do not turn the side of your face toward them, as is the habit of the arrogant. Ṣa'ar (الصَّعَر) is a condition that afflicts the camel, whereby its neck is twisted sideways. It was also read as (وَلا تُصاعِرْ) and as (وَلا تُصْعِرْ) in the causative form (al-if'al), and all of these carry the same meaning, like ʿalāhu, ʿālāhu and aʿlāhu (all meaning "he raised it" or "he overcame him").

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾ That is: joyfully. Maraḥan (مَرَحًا) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), or a verbal noun emphasizing a verb that is itself the state, meaning: you strut with strutting, or for the sake of exultation and insolence.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ This is a justification for the prohibition, or what necessitates it. The mention of "boaster" (fakhūr) after "arrogant" (mukhtāl), though it corresponds to the one who turns his cheek away, while "arrogant" corresponds to the one who walks exultantly, is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (al-fawāṣil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 19:

﴿And moderate your pace in your walking﴾, after refraining from arrogance in it; that is, be balanced between slow plodding (al-dabib) and hastening. It is also reported from him (ﷺ): "Hastening in walking removes the radiance (bahaa') of the believer." And 'A'isha's statement about 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, was: "When he walked, he hastened." Thus what is meant is more than the plodding of one feigning weakness. It is also read with a hamza (qat' al-hamza) from aqsada, as an archer is said to aqsada when he aims his arrow straight at the target (al-ramiyya).

﴿And lower your voice﴾, that is, diminish it and reduce it.

﴿Indeed, the most hideous of voices﴾, that is, the most frightful of them.

﴿is the voice of donkeys﴾: this is a justification for the command, in the most emphatic and forceful manner. It is based on likening those who raise their voices to donkeys, and representing their voices by the braying (nahiq), with exaggeration in warning against raising the voice and in repelling from it. The word "voice" (sawt) is used in the singular though it is attached to a plural noun because the intent is not to describe the voice of each individual member of this kind, which would call for the plural, but rather to describe the voice of this kind among the voices of all other kinds. And His, the Exalted's, statement:

﴿Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth?﴾ This returns to the pattern of address to the polytheists that preceded the story of Luqman, and it rebukes them for their persistence in what they were upon, despite their witnessing the proofs of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). By "subjection" (*taskhir*) is meant either making the subjected thing such that it benefits the one for whom it is subjected, in the general sense: whether it is submissive to him, so that he disposes of it as he wishes and uses it as he desires, as with most of what is on earth of the things subjected to humans and used by them, from inanimate matter and animals; or it is not like that, but rather it is a means for the attainment of his purpose without having any role in its use, as with all of what is in the heavens of things upon which the interests of the servants, in this life and the next, depend, and what He made submissive and subdued to the command. This is based on the meaning of "for you" (*lakum*) being "for your sake." For all of what is in the heavens and the earth of created beings is subjected to Allah, the Exalted, and is made to serve the benefits of creation. What a human uses as he wishes, even though it is subjected to him in outward appearance, is in reality subjected to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And He has completed His blessings upon you, outward and inward﴾, perceptible and intelligible, known to you and unknown. The explanation and detail of "blessing" has already passed in al-Fatihah. It is read *(asbagh)* with a *sad*, and this applies to every *sin* that is adjacent to a *ghayn*, a *kha'*, or a *qaf*, as you say *salakha* as *salakha*, *saqara* as *saqara*, and *saligh* as *saligh*. It is also read *(ni'mah)* in the singular.

﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah﴾ concerning His oneness and His attributes ﴿without knowledge﴾ derived from any proof, ﴿nor guidance﴾ from the Messenger ﷺ, ﴿nor an illuminating Book﴾ sent down by Allah, glory be to Him; rather, merely by blind imitation (*taqlid*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 21:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ i.e., to those who argue. The plural is according to the sense (ma'na).

﴿"Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ By this they mean the worship of idols.

﴿"Even though Shaytan (Satan) was calling them﴾ i.e., their fathers, not themselves, as has been said. For the basis of the denial of following and the deeming of it far-fetched is that the ones being followed were followers of Shaytan, not that they themselves were so. That is, "would they follow them?" Even if Shaytan was calling them to what they were upon of polytheism.﴿

﴿"...to the punishment of the Blaze"﴾ So they are heading toward it according to his call. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). Its verification has already passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And if their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?"﴾ from Surat al-Baqarah, with what there is no need to add to.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 22:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ by entrusting to Him the totality of his affairs and turning to Him wholly. Where it is construed with the preposition lam (li), the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtisas) is intended. It is also read with tashdid (doubling of the letter, as in "yuslim" pronounced with emphasis).

﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ i.e., in his deeds, performing them in a manner combining inherent goodness (husn dhati) and attributed goodness (husn wasfi). This has already been discussed at the end of Surah an-Nahl.

﴿has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾ i.e., he has clung to the most secure of the means to which one can cling. This is a parable for the state of one who relies upon Allah and occupies himself with obedience, likened to the state of one who wishes to ascend to the peak of a lofty mountain and grasps the strongest loops of the rope hanging down from it.

﴿And to Allah﴾ not to anyone else ﴿is the outcome of all affairs﴾ so He will reward him with the best of rewards.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 23:

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you﴾: for it does not harm you, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. And it has been read as (fa-la yuḥzinka) from aḥzana, derived from ḥazina with the vowel of the zāy being kasra, but it is not widely attested (laysa bi-mustafīḍ).

﴿To Us is their return﴾: not to other than Us. ﴿Then We will inform them of what they did﴾ in the world of disbelief and sins, by punishment and retribution. The plural in the three pronouns is in consideration of the meaning of "man" (min), just as the singular in the first is in consideration of its wording (lafẓ).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾: this is a justification for the "informing," which is expressed by punishment.

"We grant them enjoyment for a little while" — that is, a brief enjoyment, or a little time, for whatever passes away, even if after a long span it is little compared to what endures.

"Then We drive them to a harsh punishment" — which weighs upon them like the weight of heavy bodies, or in which constriction and compression are added to the burning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 25:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ (This is) because the matter is so manifest that they are compelled to acknowledge it.

﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah."﴾ (This is) because He has made the proofs of monotheism such that even the obstinate hardly deny them.

﴿But most of them do not know.﴾ They know nothing of (the relevant) things, and therefore they do not act in accordance with what their acknowledgment requires. It has also been said: they do not know that this (acknowledgment) entails (obligations) upon them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 26:**

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾; so none other than Him deserves worship within them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from the worlds.

﴿The Praiseworthy﴾: the one who deserves to be praised, even if no one praises Him. Or, the one who is praised in act, whom every created being praises by the tongue of its state.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 27:

﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ That is: if the trees were pens. The singular "tree" (shajarah) is used because the intent is to detail individual units.

﴿and the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it﴾ That is: after its exhaustion.

﴿seven seas﴾ That is: while the encompassing sea, despite its vastness, is replenished by the seven seas with a flow that never ceases at all. The words of Allah were written with those pens and that ink.

﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted.﴾ Those pens would be exhausted, and the ink too, as in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾. It was also read as "yamudduhu" from the causative (imdad), with the ya' and the ta'. The attribution of the replenishing to the seven seas rather than the encompassing sea, despite its being greater and more expansive, is because they are the ones adjoining the mountains and the sources of flowing waters, and into them the great rivers first pour, and from them they pour into the encompassing sea second. The use of the paucal plural (jam' qillah) for "words" serves to indicate that what has been mentioned does not suffice even for a few of them, so how about the many? ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾ nothing can overpower Him.

﴿Wise﴾ no matter escapes His knowledge and wisdom, so His words, founded upon these two, will never be exhausted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 28:

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but like that of a single soul.﴾ That is: they are not but like its creation and its resurrection in ease of accomplishment, since no matter occupies Him to the exclusion of another matter. This is because the basis of the existence of all things is the connection of His necessary will together with His essential power, as His words, exalted is He, make clear: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ who hears everything that is heard.

﴿Seeing﴾ who sees everything that is seen, whose knowledge of some things does not distract Him from knowledge of others. So likewise is creation and resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 29:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ It has been said: the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It has also been said: it is general, addressed to everyone who is fit to be addressed, and this is the more suitable reading in light of what precedes and what follows. That is: "Do you not know" with a firm knowledge, which is treated as sight (al-ru'yah).

﴿That God causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ That is: He makes each of them enter into the other and adds to it, so that its condition varies by increase and decrease.

﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "causes to enter" (yuliju). The difference in form between the two is a sign that the entering of one of the two luminaries into the other is renewed at every moment, whereas the subjugation of the two lights is a matter that has neither multiplicity nor renewal. Multiplicity and renewal occur only in its effects, and this has been indicated where it says: ﴿each runs﴾, that is, according to its particular motion and its forced motion over the varying daily orbits, which are multiple according to the multiplicity of days, running in continuous motion.

﴿for a term appointed﴾ God the Exalted has determined it for their running, and it is the Day of Resurrection, as has been related from al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him. Their running does not cease except at that time. The clause, on the supposition that the address is general, is a parenthetical insertion between the two coordinated items, to explain the actual state of affairs by way of digression. On the supposition that it is specific to him (ﷺ), it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the sun and the moon, since their running until the Day of Resurrection is among the things within the scope of his (ﷺ) sight. Their running has been taken as an expression for their particular motion in their own orbits, and the appointed term as the endpoint of their revolution. The duration of the running has been taken as one year for the sun and one month for the moon. Thus the clause then serves as an explanation of the ruling on their subjugation and as an alert to the manner of the entering of one of the two luminaries into the other. This occurs according to the variation in the running of the sun over its daily orbits: whenever its running is directed toward the zenith of the head, the arc above the earth grows larger, so the day lengthens by the joining of some parts of the night to it, until it reaches the orbit nearest to the zenith, which is when it reaches the head of Cancer. Then it turns back, moving away from the zenith, and the arcs above the earth continue to diminish, so the day shortens by the joining of some of its parts to the night, until it reaches the orbit farthest from the zenith among the daily orbits, which is when it reaches the Tropic of Capricorn (burj al-Jady).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that God is Aware of what you do﴾ is coordinated upon "That God causes to enter..." etc. It falls together with it within the scope of sight, on both suppositions of specific and general address, for whoever witnesses such an exquisite work and such a superlative arrangement can hardly be heedless that its Maker, mighty and majestic, encompasses both its great deeds and its subtle details.

**That** refers to the noble verses that come after it, and the sense of distance in it indicates the high rank of those verses in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿that God, He is the Truth﴾, meaning: by way of showing that He, may He be exalted, is the Truth—His divinity alone is true—and on account of the fact that these verses speak to the truth of monotheism.

﴿And that what they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾, meaning: and for the sake of demonstrating the falsehood of the divinity of whatever they invoke besides Him, may He be exalted, since these verses bear clear witness to this, a witness in which there is no doubt. It is also read with the ta' (i.e., "what they call upon" as "tad'una," in the second person). The explicit statement of this, although the indication that the divinity of truth belongs exclusively to Him, may He be exalted, necessarily entails the indication of the falsehood of the divinity of anything other than Him, is in order to display complete concern with the matter of monotheism, and to indicate that the indication of the falsehood of what has been mentioned is not only by way of entailment but also by way of independent proof.

﴿And that God, He is the Most High, the Great﴾, meaning: and the demonstration that He, may He be exalted, is the One who is exalted above everything and dominant over it. For what is within the folds of the noble verses clarifies that loftiness and greatness belong exclusively to Him, may He be exalted; that is, the demonstration of this. It has also been said that "that" refers to what has been mentioned of the breadth of knowledge, the comprehensiveness of power, the wonders of creation, and the exclusivity of the Creator, may He be exalted, to it, because He is the One whose existence is established in His essence, necessary from all aspects, or whose divinity is established. But you know that His truth, His exaltedness and His greatness, although they are suitable to be the ground (munatiyya) of the rulings enumerated, yet the falsehood of the divinity of the idols has no bearing on that ground at all. Therefore there is no justification for placing it in the same series of causes; rather, that is a reversal of the matter, since the rulings mentioned are what necessitate its falsehood, not that its falsehood necessitates them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 31:

"Have you not seen that the ship sails on the sea by the blessing of Allah" — by His kindness in preparing its means. This is another testimony to His manifest power, the ultimate of His wisdom, and the comprehensiveness of His bounty. The "ba'" (bi, "by") is either connected to "tajri" (sails), or to an implied element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its agent, meaning: accompanied by His blessing, exalted is He. It has been read as "al-fulka" with a damma on the lam, and as "bi-ni'mati Allah" (in the plural). The ʿayn of the pattern fiʿlat permits kasra, fatha, and sukun.

﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾, meaning: some of the indications of His oneness, His knowledge, and His power. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾ is a causal explanation of what precedes it, meaning: indeed, in what has been mentioned there are signs great in themselves and numerous in their count, for everyone who is extremely patient in hardships, so that he exhausts himself in reflecting on the souls and the horizons, and who is extremely thankful for His favours; and these two are the attributes of the believer, so it is as if it were said: for every believer.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 32:

﴿And when a wave covers them⦆ — i.e., rises over them and encompasses them.

﴿like shadows (ẓulal)⦆ — as when something overshadows them, such as a mountain, a cloud, or other things. It has also been read as (kal-ẓilāl), the plural of ẓullah (ẓullah being like qullah, and qilāl like qilāl).

﴿they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion⦆ — because of the removal of what contends with the innate nature (fitrah) from desire and blind imitation, by reason of the calamities and hardships that have befallen them.

﴿Then when He brings them safely to land, some of them are moderate (muqtaṣid)⦆ — i.e., they remain upon the upright course (al-qaṣd al-sawiyy), which is monotheism, or they are moderate in disbelief, being restrained in general terms.

﴿And none denies Our signs except every treacherous (khattār), ungrateful one⦆ — a treacherous betrayer, for this is a breaking of the covenant of innate nature, or a rejection of what was in the sea. Khatr (treachery) is the most severe and most reprehensible form of betrayal.

﴿ungrateful (kafūr)⦆ — intensive in denying the blessings of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 33:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no father will avail anything for his son.﴾ Meaning: he will not settle anything on his behalf (lā yaqḍī ʿanhu). It has also been read as (lā yujzī), from ajzaʾa, meaning "to suffice," and the returning pronoun to the described noun is omitted, meaning: no one will be recompensed in it (lā yujzā fīhi).

﴿Nor will a son avail anything for his father﴾ is coordinated with "a father" (wa-lā mawlūd ʿaṭf ʿalā "wālid"), or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿he will avail anything for his father﴾ (huwa jāz ʿan wālidihi shayʾan). The change in the structure (taghyīr al-naẓm) serves to indicate that the son is even more deserving of not being able to avail anything, and it cuts off the hope of those among the believers who expected that their unbelieving father might benefit from them in the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed, the promise of God﴾ regarding reward and punishment

﴿is true﴾, it is impossible for it to be broken at all. ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you about God﴾, meaning: Satan, who is extremely deceptive, by leading you into sins by making them appear attractive to you, and by holding out to you the hope of repentance and forgiveness. (p-78)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 31, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾: the knowledge of the time of its establishment. This is because it is narrated that al-Harith ibn 'Amr came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "When is the Hour? I have cast my seeds into the earth. When will the sky rain? Is my wife's pregnancy a male or a female? What will I do tomorrow? Where will I die?" So this was revealed. And from him (ﷺ) it is narrated: "The keys of the unseen are five," and he recited this verse: ﴿And He sends down the rain﴾ at its appointed time that He has decreed, and to its appointed place that He has determined in His knowledge. It is also read: (yunzilu) from al-inzal (causing to descend).

﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾: whether male or female, complete or incomplete.

﴿And no soul knows﴾ of souls ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾ of good or evil. It may resolve upon one of these and then do the opposite of it.

﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, just as it does not know at what time it will die.

It is narrated that the Angel of Death passed by Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and began to gaze at one of his companions who was looking at him intently. The man said: "Who is this?" He said: "The Angel of Death." The man said: "It seems he wants me. Order the wind to carry me and cast me in the land of India." So he did so. Then the angel said to Sulayman, peace be upon them both: "My continued gaze at him was out of amazement, since I had been commanded to take his soul in India, and he was with you."

The attribution of knowledge to Allah, the Exalted, and of awareness (dirayah) to the servant, is to indicate that if he exerts his stratagems and spends his utmost effort in seeking knowledge, he still does not know what will befall him of his earnings and its outcome. How then could he know other things for which no sign has been set up for him? It is also read: (bi-ayyati ardin). Sibawayh likened the feminization of it (ard) to the feminization of kull in kullatihinna.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ʿAlim﴾: intensely knowing, so nothing escapes His knowledge of things, among which is what has been mentioned.

﴿Khabir﴾: He knows their inner aspects just as He knows their outer aspects.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Luqman, Luqman will be his companion on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be given ten good deeds for each person who acted upon what is good and forbade what is evil."
